Is the two-stage correction available for a fit

Source: R/twostage.R
mc_two_stage_available.Rd

Reports which of the two routes that propagate the first-stage uncertainty into the graph layer apply to a fit, and if one does not, why. The shortcut is the reduced form evaluated at the fitted covariance (see the section "Propagating the first stage" of mc_vcov_graph). The reduced form needs every response to carry a single dispersion parameter that multiplies its variance function, \(v_{ri}=\tau_{r}V_r(\mu_{ri};p_r)\), an identity within-response structure and constant prior weights, because together they make the first-stage Pearson equations fix the average of the squared residuals of each response and let the correction be written, to first order, with second-stage quantities alone. It also needs the first stage to estimate the correlation between responses without restriction, which mcglm does and the check therefore does not read. The check below is that structural one: on a DAG with an immorality the shortcut can qualify and still be, for the parameters of the collider and of its descendants, only a first-order approximation to the reduced form, which is one of the two cases in which method = "auto" takes the full form when it is available. The other is a first stage with a variance function other than "constant": the shortcut then rests on conditions on the mean and on the residual covariance that the fit does not show (see the section "What the check cannot verify"). The full form needs only that the first stage be a sum over units, which is what the rows are when the within-response structure is the identity, and what the clusters must be otherwise.

Usage

mc_two_stage_available(fit, cluster = NULL)

Arguments

fit

an object of class "mcglm_graph".

cluster

optional vector with one identifier per observational row, as in mc_vcov_graph; default NULL. It changes only whether the full form is available for a within-response structure that is not the identity, and with it the route method = "auto" takes on a DAG with an immorality or on a fit with a variance function other than "constant".

Value

A list with shortcut_ok (logical) and why_shortcut (character vector, empty when the shortcut applies), the verdict and the reasons for the shortcut; full_ok and why_full, the same for the full form; and method, a string, "shortcut" or "full", the route method = "auto" takes in mc_vcov_graph(type = "two_stage") and in the functions that consume it, or NA_character_ when neither applies. The shortcut can apply (shortcut_ok = TRUE) while method is "full": "auto" takes the full form, when it is available, for a fit with a variance function other than "constant" and for a DAG with an immorality. The components ok and why repeat shortcut_ok and why_shortcut.

Which fits qualify for the shortcut

The variance functions "constant", "tweedie", "binomialP" and "binomialPQ" are multiplicative in the dispersion parameter and qualify. "poisson_tweedie" is additive, \(v=\mu+\tau\mu^{p}\), and qualifies only at \(p=1\), where it collapses to \((1+\tau)\mu\); the power must be fixed there rather than estimated, since an estimated power is a first-stage parameter of its own. A response with more than one covariance component has more than one dispersion parameter and does not qualify. Prior weights must be constant: with weights that vary, the first stage fixes a weighted average of the squared residuals rather than their average.

A single dispersion parameter is necessary and not sufficient. The identity comes from the first-stage equations being the score of a working Gaussian model that factorizes over units, which needs the within-response structure to be a multiple of the identity. One covariance component that is not diagonal keeps the parameter count at one and breaks the factorization all the same, so it is refused too.

Which fits qualify for the full form

Any family, any number of covariance components and any power, estimated or fixed, provided the fit carries its first-stage components and the graph layer sits on its Pearson residuals. With an identity within-response structure the units are the rows, or the clusters when cluster is given. With any other structure cluster is required and has to nest it: every matrix of the matrix linear predictor must vanish between rows of distinct clusters, which is checked. A random-effect block per subject nested in a cluster per hunter, say, qualifies with the hunter as the cluster.

What the check cannot verify

The check reads the structure of the first-stage fit and nothing else: the variance functions, the number of dispersion parameters, whether the within-response structure is the identity or nests in the clusters, whether a Poisson-Tweedie power was fixed at one and whether the prior weights are constant. For the shortcut, that structure makes the first stage fix the average of the squared residuals, which is the algebraic half of it. The statistical half, that the first stage moves the residual covariance along a diagonal rescaling, rests on statements about the data that cannot be read off the fit:

  • a correctly specified mean, condition (b) of the section "What the correction reaches" of mc_vcov_graph. It is not needed when all responses have the same design, with an intercept, and the derivative of the mean in the linear predictor divided by the standard deviation is the same for every unit, as with the constant variance function and the identity link, or with the Tweedie variance function of power fixed at two and the log link;

  • a conditional residual covariance that does not depend on the covariates, condition (c) there. It is not needed, whatever the link, when every response has the constant variance function; a variance function that depends on the mean needs it at least in the weaker form of conditional second moments of the Pearson residuals that change with the covariates only through a factor common to the responses;

  • independence between the units, that is between the rows once the within-response structure is the identity, or between the clusters.

The first two concern the shortcut only; the full form, with its observed sensitivity, does not need them. The third concerns every form. A fit can pass the check and still violate them. The spatial example is the plain case: a soil survey fitted with a trend surface in the mean and an identity within-response structure qualifies, while its neighboring sites remain dependent, since coordinates in the mean do not whiten the residuals. There the rows are not independent units, and neither the corrected form nor the sandwich it corrects has the variance it claims.

Since the first two cannot be verified, and the constant variance function is the case that does not need the second, method = "auto" takes the full form, when it is available, for a fit in which some response has another variance function.

References

Murphy, K. M. and Topel, R. H. (1985). Estimation and inference in two-step econometric models. Journal of Business and Economic Statistics 3(4), 370–379. doi:10.1080/07350015.1985.10509471

Newey, W. K. and McFadden, D. (1994). Large sample estimation and hypothesis testing. In Engle, R. F. and McFadden, D. L. (eds), Handbook of Econometrics, vol. 4, 2111–2245. Elsevier. doi:10.1016/S1573-4412(05)80005-4

See also

mc_vcov_graph, whose type = "two_stage" consumes this check, and mc_graph_bootstrap, which propagates the first stage by refitting.

Other inference on the graph layer: mc_test_adequacy(), mc_test_independence(), mc_vcov_graph(), mc_wald_graph()

Examples

# \donttest{
set.seed(1); n <- 200; x <- rnorm(n)
d <- data.frame(y1 = rnorm(n), y2 = rnorm(n), y3 = rnorm(n), x = x)
f <- mcglm_graph(list(y1 ~ x, y2 ~ x, y3 ~ x), data = d)
#> Automatic initial values selected.
mc_two_stage_available(f)
#> $ok
#> [1] TRUE
#> 
#> $why
#> character(0)
#> 
#> $shortcut_ok
#> [1] TRUE
#> 
#> $why_shortcut
#> character(0)
#> 
#> $full_ok
#> [1] TRUE
#> 
#> $why_full
#> character(0)
#> 
#> $method
#> [1] "shortcut"
#> 
# }
